title: Coordinate Geometry Formulas

findings.finding: The midpoint topic has no opening review of signed addition and formula substitution, both used directly in its introductory examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must substitute signed values into corresponding positions and evaluate signed sums while learning the midpoint formula. Neither prerequisite is rehearsed before these examples.
findings.checked: All supplied teaching was checked. This is the first topic, and it contains no review. Both introductory examples require substitution and signed addition.
findings.assumptions: These are prior skills, consistent with the course library. Calculator availability does not remove the substitution requirement.

repair.proposal: Before p3-formula, add: (a) Calculate -4+8. (b) Calculate 3+(-5). (c) Given F=(a+b)/2, substitute a=-6 and b=10 and evaluate F. (d) Given G=(c+d)/2, substitute c=2 and d=-7 and evaluate G. Answers: 4, -2, 2, -2.5.

findings.doneWhen: A short opening review rehearses signed addition and substitution before the midpoint teaching.

findings.finding: Unequal division requires a coordinate calculation that the preceding teaching does not supply.
findings.breakdown: Parts p7-q8-a and b identify the fraction of each displacement, but do not explain adding that fractional displacement to the starting coordinate. Students may instead multiply B's coordinates by the fraction.
findings.checked: The complete preceding teaching supplies midpoint averaging and inverse midpoint practice, but no unequal-division calculation. The diagram and fraction questions identify the displacement fraction without showing the coordinate offset.
findings.assumptions: Ratio-to-fraction conversion and basic signed arithmetic are prior knowledge; unequal coordinate division is a new variant.

repair.proposal: Between p7-q8-b and c, add: 'Start at A and add one third of the change from A to B in each coordinate. For x: x_P=-3+(1/3)[3-(-3)]=-1. Use the same method for y.' Leave students to calculate y and assemble P.

findings.doneWhen: Students see start + fraction × signed coordinate change before completing the unequal-division tasks.

findings.finding: Compare complementary division points with the midpoint of their original segment.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects unequal division with midpoint averaging using the existing endpoints.
findings.checked: For A=(-2,-3) and B=(4,0), P=(8/5,-6/5) and Q=(2/5,-9/5). Both midpoint calculations give (1,-3/2). The task uses only midpoint and unequal-division methods.
findings.assumptions: Place this after the unequal-division teaching repair.

repair.proposal: Append to p7-q10: (b) Find Q when AQ:QB=2:3. Answer: (2/5,-9/5). (c) Find the midpoint of PQ. Answer: (1,-3/2). (d) Find the midpoint of AB. Answer: (1,-3/2). (e) Explain why the two midpoints agree. Expected answer: P and Q are three fifths and two fifths of the way from A to B, so their average position is halfway along AB.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up retains the existing segment and separates each question into its own part.

findings.finding: A short sequence can connect changing vertical displacement with positive, zero and negative gradients.
findings.breakdown: Holding the first endpoint and horizontal displacement fixed makes the effect of the second y-coordinate visible.
findings.checked: The proposed gradients are 1, 1/2, 0, -1/2 and -1; the unpatterned follow-up has gradient -3/2. Every denominator is nonzero. Existing gradient practice contains no comparable run.
findings.assumptions: The stated gradient formula suffices for all proposed parts.

repair.proposal: Append to p9-q1 the single instruction 'Predict how the gradient will change before calculating.' Add g (1,2) and (5,6); h (1,2) and (5,4); i (1,2) and (5,2); j (1,2) and (5,0); k (1,2) and (5,-2). Answers: 1, 1/2, 0, -1/2, -1. Follow with l (-2,5) and (4,-4), answer -3/2. Across g–k, only the second y-coordinate varies.

findings.doneWhen: The run and its unpatterned follow-up appear under the existing gradient instruction, with only one added prediction line.

findings.finding: Parts c and d repeat the same whole distance task without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both ask for the exact distance between (0,0) and (-6,-8), with identical instructions and no additional givens or diagrams.
findings.checked: The complete shared stem and both endpoint pairs match. No retrieval or comparison purpose distinguishes the copies.
findings.assumptions: No unstated purpose is inferred for the identical tasks.
findings.doneWhen: The later copy has different coordinates while retaining the same task structure.

findings.finding: The first inverse-distance question combines reversing the radical formula with recovering both signs of an unknown difference.
findings.breakdown: Earlier distance questions only evaluate known coordinates. Here students must form an equation from the given distance, square both sides, isolate a squared difference and retain two coordinate values. Earlier inverse-midpoint practice does not bridge these additional decisions.
findings.checked: All preceding distance teaching and practice were checked; none reverses the distance formula. In part a, 8=4+(5-a)^2 gives a=3 or 7. In part b, 29=(4-a)^2+4 gives a=-1 or 9.
findings.assumptions: Basic equation solving and solving square equations are prior knowledge. The gap concerns their combined application to this formula and does not depend on calculator availability.

repair.proposal: Add to p14-q5-a: 'Start with √8=√((3-1)²+(5-a)²). Square both sides and isolate (5-a)². Remember: if u²=4, then u=2 or -2.' Leave students to finish and apply the method independently in part b.

findings.doneWhen: The first inverse-distance task supplies an equation-starting cue and prompts both signs.

findings.finding: Group the existing reflection cases to make their equal distances easier to compare.
findings.breakdown: The supplied order separates the cases. A consecutive run exposes how squaring removes the signs of the coordinate differences.
findings.checked: After the duplicate repair, the four origin-based cases all have distance 10. The proposed unpatterned pair has squared distance 25+64=89. No new method is required.
findings.assumptions: Use the replacement for p12-q2-d from c7; reuse existing cases rather than adding copies.

repair.proposal: At the start of p12-q2, place consecutively the pairs (0,0) and (6,8); (0,0) and (-6,8); (0,0) and (-6,-8); (0,0) and (6,-8). Add only: 'Predict which distances will be equal before calculating.' Answers: 10 each. Follow with (2,-3) and (7,5), answer √89, then the remaining existing parts.

findings.doneWhen: The four reflection cases form one run followed by an unpatterned task, with only one added prediction line.

findings.finding: Use the midpoint of the tied closest points as a further distance comparison.
findings.breakdown: This concrete follow-up connects the booklet's midpoint and distance methods.
findings.checked: B=(-1,-1) and C=(-3,3) have midpoint M=(-2,1). Its distance from (2,3) is √20≈4.47, less than the distance 5 for either B or C.
findings.assumptions: Midpoint and distance calculations are available by this point.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p13-q3-root: (a) Find the midpoint M of B and C. Answer: (-2,1). (b) Find the distance from M to (2,3). Answer: √20≈4.47 units. (c) Which is closest to (2,3): B, C or M? Answer: M.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts follow the existing closest-point question and use its coordinates.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing both endpoint assignments preserves the gradient.
protectedGroups.invariant: The two points, the line and its gradient.

protectedGroups.observation: The same distance is retained when coordinate differences change sign or the interval moves.
protectedGroups.varies: Endpoint positions and signs of the differences.

protectedGroups.observation: Translating an interval preserves its length.
Reversing endpoint order leaves the midpoint unchanged; this adjacent comparison provides an instructional reason for repeating the endpoint pair.
protectedGroups.invariant: The two endpoints and their midpoint

protectedGroups.observation: Changing one endpoint coordinate changes only the corresponding midpoint coordinate.
protectedGroups.varies: One coordinate sign at each step
protectedGroups.invariant: The other three endpoint coordinates at each step

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the fixed endpoint's coordinate signs affects the corresponding midpoint coordinates independently.
protectedGroups.varies: First the x sign, then the y sign of one endpoint
protectedGroups.invariant: The other endpoint and all coordinate magnitudes

protectedGroups.observation: Scaling both endpoints by ten scales the midpoint by ten.
protectedGroups.invariant: Endpoint proportions, signs and vertical alignment

importReview: Lean content review table: 34 of 34 blocks passed.

dropped.reason: The unsupported-method test defeats this candidate. The midpoint formula explicitly identifies M as the result, and the candidate assumes students already know how to solve the resulting simple linear equations. The table introduces one change—an unknown endpoint—using those existing methods; the absence of an earlier inverse worked setup alone does not establish an unsupported transition or a sharp jump.

candidates.finding: The first missing-endpoint question precedes the sequence's only explicit setup of an inverse-midpoint equation.

dropped.reason: The immediately preceding topic's practice defeats the missing-review claim. Inverse midpoint tasks already require signed subtraction, including subtracting negatives: p6-q4-row4 uses 4-(-1), and p6-q6-d uses -3-(-5). The subsequent ratio-division tasks also use signed coordinate differences. This prerequisite therefore need not be reviewed again at the gradient opening.

candidates.finding: The topic has no opening rehearsal of signed subtraction, although its second introductory example depends directly on subtracting negative coordinates.
